planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cool, partly sunny site.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cool, partly sunny site, recreating the snowmelt-fed subalpine meadows of the Cascade and Olympic Mountains where it forms low, spreading mats. Bell-shaped pink flowers appear in early summer followed by sweet, powder-blue berries considered among the best-flavored of the wild huckleberries and are eagerly sought by birds, bears, and foragers alike. It resents summer drought and heat, so it performs best in cool-climate gardens or high-elevation native plantings with reliable soil moisture.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant young transplants in spring into acidic, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full to partial sun.

directions: Plant young transplants in spring into acidic, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full to partial sun, matching the boreal barrens, subalpine meadows, and lakeshores across its wide transcontinental range from Alaska to New England. This low, tufted shrub bears small white-to-pink flowers in late spring followed by sweet, dark blue berries relished by grouse, songbirds, and small mammals. Its compact, mat-forming habit makes it a good choice for a sunny native rock garden or as a groundcover at the front of an acidic border.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun; use only nursery-propagated plants since natural populations are globally rare.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun, reproducing the coastal heathlands and pine barrens from Newfoundland to New Jersey where this rare, fire-adapted shrub grows alongside bearberry and lowbush blueberry. Its needle-like evergreen foliage and inconspicuous, wind-pollinated flowers in earliest spring give it a heath-like texture that fills a distinct niche in a dry, sandy native planting. Because natural populations are globally rare and disturbance-dependent, use only nursery-propagated plants and avoid rich or moisture-retentive soils that this dune and barrens specialist will not tolerate.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained gritty soil in a cool site with some afternoon shade.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained gritty soil in a cool site with some afternoon shade, mimicking the snowmelt-fed subalpine and alpine meadows of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada, and northern Rockies. Its heather-like needle foliage and nodding, bell-shaped pink flowers in early summer make it a favorite for high-elevation rock gardens and are visited by native bumblebees. It needs consistent moisture through the growing season and cool nights, so it is best suited to mountain or maritime climate gardens rather than hot lowland sites.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site, recreating the high alpine and subalpine slopes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it often grows beside its pink-flowered relative. Clusters of small, urn-shaped, greenish-yellow to cream flowers open in early summer above dense needle-like foliage, and where the two species overlap they hybridize into an intermediate-colored form. Give it steady moisture and cool summers; it declines quickly in hot, dry, or poorly drained garden conditions.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
